Preface: the shelfmark is printed as 328 A and 3288 A; read 3288 A. 'in his med(??)is commentariis' is damaged; read as 'meis' ('these commentaries of mine'). Scanning errors read as: proepostium = praepositum, pali = pati, factat = faciat, nui = uni, proteram = proferam, Samondo = Sirmondo, herivallensis = Herivallensis (Herivaux). In I, 'admittant' is taken as 'amittant' ('give up'). In III, 'id egit quod numquam' appears elliptical or defective; the supplement is conjectural. 'innata' is rendered 'unborn' (ungenerated).

Line 5: 'stare suum facere non potuerint' and 'nec ipsi suum regunt, sed usus' are obscure and probably corrupt; rendered by sense. The final 'non esse' is taken as 'is not [a god]'. Line 6: 'neutrum' though three alternatives are listed; rendered 'none'. 'fotura ficri' read as 'futura fieri'. Line 7: 'ni simus' read as 'ut simus'. Line 8: 'culpnra' read as 'culpam'; 'positus fruebatur' rendered 'once placed [there], he enjoyed'. Line 9: 'Caetera' taken as 'Caeterum' (for the rest).

XI 'Judicio maximo' may stand for 'judicio maxime'. XII 'rerum esse Dominum peccati' seems defective; translated as ascribing the sin to the Lord of all things as its cause. XIV 'concitur' read as 'vincitur' (overcome). XV 'non poenitentiae' read as 'non poenitenti'; 'expetit' taken as 'competit' (belongs to); 'sentiens humo se liberatum sententia praesentis' read as 'sentiens homo ... sententia praesenti'; 'motus tamen tamquam index cogitationum aliquo sociando' is obscure and possibly corrupt.

XVI: ‘spinarum substantia, maledictam’ is ungrammatical and probably corrupt; translated as it stands. XVII: ‘propter caeteros’ read as ‘praeter caeteros’ and ‘cante’ as ‘caute’; ‘sed quod deerat in natura gignentis, mater ei sit virgo’ is obscure and translated literally. XVIII: ‘in venio austro’ read as ‘in vento austro’. XIX: ‘seminas paludium’ uncertain, perhaps for ‘sentinas’ (foul or bilge waters); ‘astringere’, here rendered ‘act upon’, normally means to bind or compact; ‘in vivo sancto, quia corpore’ read as ‘in vivo sancto corpore’. XXI: the edition’s punctuation ‘sociator gloriae. et pacis effector’ taken as ‘sociator, gloriae et pacis effector’.

XXIII: 'nostra causa liberationis' is awkward; rendered 'for the sake of our liberation'. XXIV: 'non esset' is elliptical, probably 'he was not [hungry]'. XXV: 'divinam prominendo' seems corrupt, perhaps 'divinam [aquam] promittendo'; rendered 'by promising'. 'Samariae' read with 'the other Samaritans'. XXVI: 'rufandis' read as 'curandis' (healing). The quoted psalm is Ps 106 (107) in the Vulgate numbering. 'spiritus potestatis' (Vulgate 'spiritus procellae') rendered 'wind of the storm'. 'questum' read as 'quaestum'. XXVII: 'coelesti impare' read as 'coelestibus impares'.

nodes.text: VICTORINUS' BOOK ON PHYSICS.
(Mai's Collection, vol. iii.)
Notice prefixed by Mai to the book On Physics.

For preparing this edition of these commentaries I have used three manuscripts of the Vatican Library: namely Ottobonianus 3288 A, of the fourteenth century, from which Ottobonianus 3288 B, of the sixteenth century, was copied; and lastly Vaticanus 3546, likewise of the sixteenth century, taken more or less from one or the other Ottobonianus. For this reason there is almost no variety of readings in these commentaries of mine; and the same gaps appear in all the manuscripts, and the same corruption, ambiguity and obscurity in very many places. Otherwise the spelling is somewhat more ancient in the first, 3288 A, which, evidently, the later copyists repeatedly altered in the other copies. Moreover, the contents of all the manuscripts are the same, namely the published and likewise the unpublished writings of Victorinus. First comes Victorinus' commentary on the Apocalypse (or *commentarium*, as it is more often written in these manuscripts), with the letter of Jerome placed before it; this little work exists under the disputed name of Victorinus of Pettau in the great Lyons Library of the Fathers, vol. iii, p. 414 ff. There follow Victorinus' commentaries, hitherto unpublished, on the letters to the Galatians and to the Philippians. Then are written two little works of Victorinus, namely on the words of Genesis, 'and there was evening and morning, one day', and Against the Two Principles of the Manichaeans; both of which Sirmond first brought to light, taken from a manuscript of the monastery of Herivaux. In that manuscript there also lay hidden commentaries of Victorinus on some of Paul's letters, which Sirmond indeed praised, and said were plainer and clearer than Victorinus' usual style (Works, vol. i, p. 345 ff.); yet he did not publish them, prevented either by various occupations, or by someone's wish, or by some other chance. However, in the Vatican manuscripts the little work against the Manichaeans lacks the first chapter, which the published text has; but in turn the published text lacks a closing passage, which I shall now bring forward. For the edition ends at 'to whom be honour and glory'. But the Vatican manuscripts have: 'to whom be honour and glory from all creatures, both before the beginnings and after the ends. Thus, then, from the true, which is, there arises also the being of the false, as shadows from solid bodies: for if there is no solid body, no shadow comes about either.' There follows in the manuscripts a commentary, hitherto unpublished, on the letter to the Ephesians. Last in the manuscripts is a little work entitled On Physics, which certainly has not been published under the name of Victorinus; whether it perhaps exists under another name, I do not know. To me it certainly seems entirely Victorinus', both because of the similarity of style, and because in these three Vatican manuscripts there is no writing except Victorinus'. And if Victorinus' name is not set before this writing, I say that that very name is not set, in these manuscripts, even before the two little works which I said were published by Sirmond, and which are without doubt Victorinus'. Therefore I have not allowed Victorinus' writing On Physics to be missing from this volume of mine.
HERE BEGINS THE BOOK ON PHYSICS.

I. Human sense knows God, the founder of all things, by natural judgement and impulse. But the physicists, marvelling at things themselves, or rather stupefied, blinded by the force of the wonder, have forgotten the very founder of the whole creation. For some contend, with a most audacious impulse, that there is no God, but that nature generates all things from itself without God. Others, acknowledging both God and nature, make the nature of things equal to God: they say indeed that he did violence to nature, in that he is taught to have fashioned [things] by appropriating from her; but again that he suffers violence, in that nature dissolves the things which he himself set up. These two kinds, opposed to each other, but both blaspheming, must be answered: and first, I think, those who are the more audacious, whom we said deny God, who is made manifest from all his creation. For who doubts that the order which is in the nature of things was set by someone, not by itself? For the seasons grant one another their measures and yield in turn; and the sun, though it is brighter and more powerful, and has the greatest strength, gives way by night to the moon and the chorus of stars, which are lesser than it, nor can it always keep the day itself in the same span; the stars and the moon give up the very span of power which they had; spring, autumn, winter and summer are expected and come in a fixed and orderly span. And yet even upon the seasons themselves force is sometimes brought, so that they do not always do what is expected, but, with something preventing [them], exceed their measure. What need is there to draw out discussion about the sea, the rivers, the earth, the mountains and the other elements, or the fruits that are born from them? Let us now approach the things that were promised.

II. Creation itself proclaims someone as its maker: for it does not, by generating itself, in turn consume itself, since the purpose of making is one thing, and that of consuming another; and if the nature of things always brought forth the whole from itself, it would also have preserved the whole; especially since those who grant it an eternal nature, without beginning, are compelled to grant it also an eternal power: and since this power is found in the things which it generates, the things generated must also be eternal and without beginning; which the daily birth of things proves to be false. And if it is said that things themselves always exist because they succeed one another, yet in individual things the limit of birth and dissolution shows that, since each one is also confined within this defect, through that very individuality the defect is fitted to all. Thus all things that have been made cannot be without limit: for they begin and are completed, they grow and decrease. From all of which someone is found who brings force upon nature, so that it always suffers this same defect.

III. Having thus learned from these physical reasons themselves, which human sense too has always acknowledged, we must now answer those who posit such a founder, so needy that he did not fashion from his own, but by appropriating another's; so that he is found not only needy but also unjust. For what had he to do with another's matter, if he could have had his own? So they seem compelled to acknowledge God, yet not to understand God's power, nor to marvel at him, since [they think] he fashioned like a man from matter set before him. They lower his dignity, as they think, so far that they themselves make matter equal to God in origin, matter which both suffers force from him and exerts it. For it suffers when it generates; it acts when it dissolves; and both are brought to nothing. Next, they must be asked whether each of the two keeps the property of its origin. For if God is overcome, he has lost his own proper power in his origin. Again, if matter is reshaped by God, it has lost the form of its origin. Then, when, once the work was begun, it did what [it had] never [done], so that it generates under compulsion from the maker, it received for a time some power from him for bringing forth. But if it received what it did not have, it is already excluded from the might of eternity by the power it received. Therefore I ask: how is that proved unborn which did not remain in the form of its origin? That which is changed in power, colour, form, quality, and all its forces cannot be in the same power nor in the same substance: that cannot be unborn which succumbs to so many defects and necessities. And since it is, and is proved, not unborn, it remains that what it is should be recognised as born and made.

IV. And it is known that not many gods, but one, made it. For reason does not allow there to be many gods on account of the diversity of things or of powers, since on a single earth diverse kinds of herbs, fruits and trees are produced, brought forth with diverse bodies, adorned with diverse colours, strengthened with diverse powers. Indeed our soul too, though it is one, establishes diverse contrivances of arts, teachings of disciplines, forms of institutions, the number of measures, the raising of sounds, the accomplishment of things, thoughts, and judgements of reasoning. And if in such very small matters so many accomplishments are granted to one substance, how much more is that divinity, the begetter of these very things, known to be one, since the diversity of things could neither bring force upon so great a majesty nor take away its power? Next it must be asked in what way they introduce many gods: whether all [are] creators of all things, or of individual things? They cannot be founders of all things, because one suffices, as has been said. But if many gods are thought to do this, all must bring to individual things what they give. Hence what is brought by one is imperfect, and matter lacks the contribution of the others, because what it received from one does not suffice. And then matter is better, since it alone has taken into itself the powers of all.

V. Next, it is not proved that individual things were established by all [the gods]: a stone does not subsist from the same [elements] as a tree, nor a tree from those of cattle, nor the race of fish from those of wild beasts, nor serpents or monsters from those of man: rather one must admit that they have less and more. Hence it is recognised that they are not all founders of individual things, nor do they reign in all things. Since they have not contributed to all things, and since diverse kinds have been contributed, and not all equal (for one differs from another), it must be recognised that they contribute less and more. From this contribution one is found greater and another lesser in his power: and this difference does not allow that a divinity of origin has been established as one for all: from which unbornness again belongs to one, the rest being excluded from unbornness; hence they must have been born. And now, being born, it is proved that they do not have what they are from themselves, nor have power from themselves, but [power] given. But if they are not from themselves, and also use a power given [to them], how will they be said to have made all things, when they themselves have been shown to be creatures? And all this applies if all contribute to individual things. But if not all, but individuals rule individual things, and one does not use the creation of another, then the whole world would be cut apart, each drawing his own works to himself and defending them, nor would we ourselves allow [anyone] to use another's creation; and how could living creatures live, each separated from the rest? But if, out of the harmony of their goodness, they permit [it], they themselves are weak, being unable to maintain their own except through another's creation; nor do they rule their own, but use [does]. But if use holds [it], he does not rule; from which it is recognised that he is not [a god].

VI. And the world itself curbs the madness of these men, showing its creator, ruler, governor, and steward. For who, sending rains upon the things of others, nourishes others' things by his own working? Who, by interposing a tempering, has joined together all the harmful contrarieties of the seasons for usefulness? [Who] supplies the blowing of the winds, for the sake of animation, to the creation of things being born? God indeed is discerned from all creation, as it is written: The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. He is found to be the founder, ruler, governor and steward of all things: and when this is known, certain people, with perverse contentiousness, not grasping the order of things through the weakness of their minds, and not understanding even this, that they do not know, cunningly heap charges upon God; either saying that [things] ought not to have been made such that they would fall, or that from the fact that they fall, ignorance or malice must be ascribed to him. For he made them to be: but if it has come about that they are not, either in making them he was ignorant of what came about; or, knowing, though willing, he was unable to free [them]; or, though able, he handed [them] over through malice. None of which is admitted in the divinity: for it is not right that the divinity should not have known the future, nor that, willing to free, it was unable, nor that malice be ascribed: he who willed and made, from the very fact that [his was] the will to make, excludes the malice of neglecting. When these are removed, they throw at God a third charge, of impotence. All of which must be explained. For he is not evil who willed and made, and because he made willingly. He who can do all things, or can do what he wills, will not be weak, just as he is not subject to ignorance: since he always is, future things cannot come to be without him.

VII. Now, therefore, let us seek the cause of things, lest by drawing out the discussion at length we leave room for error to seducers. He made all things so that they might be: this we profess without doubt. It has come about that they are not: this too we cannot deny. But contraries cannot exist in the same [being], so that it should befall his will both to be and not to be at once. For if he made [them] to be, he always wills that they be: and if he wills that they not be, he ceases to will what he was willing; and this defect cannot befall God. Now, since two persons are set in the case, the founder and the founded, and since the founder is free from the charge, it remains that what was founded is itself the cause of its own injury, and that it could not have fallen into not being without some fault. Again, if the fault of the founded made void the will of God, the fault itself [would be] stronger than the founder: and therefore it is necessary to be reborn, so that, coming to him as what we were, we may make void what came about through fault; and the will of God, which was that we should be, may prevail. Hence, condemned for fault, we are called back, the justice of God remaining the same, and his power: justice, in that he judges; power, in that he calls back: he is not prevented from saving, who is mighty, so that he can call back, out of what has fallen, what he himself had made from nothing: and he who made from nothing will much more call back from something: and as [man] fell condemned by God's word in just judgement, so let him rise again by the word of his mercy: nor is he barred from calling back who always is; and his power obeys his will, and justice [obeys] power: and with power accomplishing [it], he does what he wills, at the time he wills, or rather at the fitting time. Nor will the death of condemnation hinder his power; nor does condemnation overcome the purpose of his will; but his mercy is not empty, nor is the grace of renewal without reason; for it is given to those who ask, just as those who did not ask were condemned.

VIII. This was the reason for not pardoning the first sinners: when, by his questioning, he called them to repentance and saw them rejecting their own salvation, he condemned them. But those who were born from them, and who took refuge in him, he pitied. For it is just that those who are willing and repentant, taking refuge in him who is able to grant [it], should obtain [it]; [and] to dismiss the ungrateful, the resisting, those who heap the blame for their own deed upon God, who have made themselves the cause of their condemnation. That justice did not permit this grace to be given to the first-formed: it was not that he who condemns was himself unwilling to grant [it]. He who is now was also before, and will be: he who is now good was also good before: he who is now merciful was also merciful before: ever remaining in this, being unchangeable: and since he condemned [man] for fault, it is necessary to discern the fault itself, which let us again inquire into by physical reasonings. Man, made not to render anything to his founder, but so that he himself might possess the world, constituted from better things, was rightly made rational: and the very reason of creation demanded this, that, diverse things having been founded in the world and constructed from the transformation of all the elements, this one, who is better than all, should have power over the rest: not then unmindful of his creator, but, subject to his lordship through a commandment, he should hold the other things subject to himself. Now the subjection of this one, who is rational, requires a law, lest he himself, the god of all things, be free from law: and since reason demands this law, we must look into the matters in which it was to be given. Reason teaches that the law was to be given in the things which, once placed [there], he enjoyed. And since food is found to be chiefly what was then given, reason demanded that the law was given concerning this, and it is declared that he sinned concerning this.

IX. Now, as we investigate the cause, reason has led us thus far. For the rest, as we inquire concerning what food, for what use, in what manner the law was given, a narrative is necessary which agrees with these physical reasonings already investigated by us: and since there is no other than what we have learned in the divine scriptures, the physical reasonings themselves leading us into that very [narrative], let us inquire whether it is consistent that a law was laid on man to abstain from one tree while enjoying the rest abundantly. Scripture teaches that he, having transgressed the commandment, was punished with death: which certain people bitterly criticise, saying that a law was given which could not be kept; that he, foreknowing the future, gave this commandment which he knew they would not keep; that he commanded abstinence from this food, the desire for which would overcome the commandment. And many other things, [they say,] are contrary to the case: for either he ought not to have given, they say, this commandment, which he gave knowing they would not observe it; or he should not have set this tree in between, like a stumbling-block to the commandment. For he could have given orders concerning the other things, in which desire did not arise, or given this precept, which man could keep. But if he could not protect him by his help from sinning, he was powerless: or else he should not have allowed the tempter to approach, by whose persuasion he fell into fault. But as it is, all the contrary things together: by making him such, he brought it about that he would be overcome; and he planted a harmful tree; and concerning it he gave a commandment which he knew they would not observe; and foreseeing by his foreknowledge that he would sin, he let him be, and did not prevent the adversary approaching to overthrow man; and, moved by anger, he himself condemned to death the one he had set [there] for life. And now you say that he has come to free him, to suffer for him, who at that time was unwilling to pardon. Such empty words they put forward from the sluggishness of their minds; all of which must be answered.

X. And indeed we have already proved that it was right for a law to be given: that he, to whom so many things had been subjected, should be subject to God through a law. This law, we teach, was not heavy, as they say, but rather light and easy to keep. For while he enjoyed all things, he was ordered to abstain from one. But if he had been ordered to use only one, with the rest forbidden, would it not seem just to you to keep the commandment of him who gave leave to enjoy [it]? Yet he who gave [the law] did not do this; though it is shown that even this would have been possible. Do we not also in this world abstain from a great many things, because of the harm of death or disease? So the commandment is shown to be possible. And if this is possible, how much more possible is it for one who enjoys all things to keep himself from one? And how could a law have been given, if it is not granted [to God] to command even in one thing? Since, then, a law had to be given, and had to be given in the things which he enjoyed, it is rightly discerned that it was given in these very things. Yet the tree was not a stumbling-block, nor ought the commandment to have passed to another [tree] rather than to this one: since in whichever [tree] the commandment had been placed, desire would have followed in that very one too. And the tree was not the occasion of desire; rather he was its author himself, who chose to desire. Nor let a complaint now arise as to why he chose, since he had power over himself, being constituted rational. The law itself also requires that the one for whom it is laid down should have this power over himself; for to one who has no power of acting, the law is void: and if someone, naturally confined by another, is seen to be restrained by that same one through a law laid down, the law is given not so much to the one prevented as to the one who keeps the confined one in check. Therefore power over himself was fittingly given: and man, having used this power, fittingly given, in that over which he had no power, is rightly condemned.

XI. Now, the sentence for transgression having been foretold by the Lord, help also had been given him, so that he might know both what he ought to beware of, and what he would suffer from negligence, if he did not beware. Nor was he weak by nature. For when the serpent approached to persuade the woman, the woman prevailed as long as she willed; and at the beginning of his words she perceived him to be a liar and repelled him, as Scripture says: And the serpent said to the woman: Why has God said, You shall not eat of every tree that is in paradise? believing he could deceive by a lie, and supposing her even to have forgotten the divine commandment. Answering him at once, she drove him off thus. And the woman said to the serpent: Of every tree that is in paradise we shall eat; but of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God said: You shall not eat of it nor touch it, lest we die. With the greatest judgement she preferred the divine command: refuted by this, he shifted to another device, saying: You shall not die the death: for God knew that on the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil. Whereupon, seized by desire for deity, she threw away what she had foreseen before; now seeing, out of lust, something other than what she [truly] saw. For then the woman says that the tree is good for food, and that it pleases the eyes; seeing from desire, not from the judgement of the mind; so that before she ate, she pronounced it good for food: and it was not the natural appearance of the tree, nor its use, that drew her, from which, on seeing it before, she had abstained; but the desire for deity enticed her.

XII. Nor need one ask why he allowed him to be tempted, whom, endowed with knowledge of the future, he had protected by his help from being deceived. But he, forgetful of his own safety and unmindful of God's words, preferring the woman's persuasions, was deceived. She indeed made her husband a partner in the sin. Upon this her husband, without questioning, received and took [it]. For she herself ate, says Scripture, and gave to her husband, and they ate. Hence the condemnation was the more just, and the judgement of death followed; for, having been warned, he did not observe [the commandment]; and when called to repentance, he not only refused, but even imputed the guilt of his deed to God, saying: The woman whom you gave me, she gave to me, and I ate; ascribing to the Lord of all things [the cause] of the sin, because he gave the woman: whereas, knowing her above all to be a small portion of his own body, to whom he had also given a name, he ought not to have submitted to her, knowing her to be in every way subject to himself; recognising himself too as the source of her body, her origin, her procreation, and even of her very name: and since he ought not to have preferred her to himself, much less [to] the Lord God who commanded. For so many crimes one sentence was given. Yet he did not judge moved by anger, as they say: for this defect cannot befall God, so that he should seem passible, so that, roused by anger, he should impose the condition of death. For he is provoked by anger who, moved by a sin, pronounces sentence: but he who proclaimed the judgement on the deed before the offence, he who warned, cannot be said to have been angry; since a warning is not anger, but protection.

XIII. Next let us see what kind of sentence he gave in the event itself. The one who ate so as to be eternal, like God, he judged that very thing by condemning [him], so that what man had supposed would come about should not come about: and whereas all food serves to strengthen the substance, this food served rather to dissolve the substance. So neither did he foretell it in hostility then, when he warned, nor did he condemn in anger afterwards, by dissolving what man had presumed. Nor did he forbid eating out of envy, nor take away deity out of envy, in forbidding the food which was harmful: for one who could not guard himself from wickedness ought not to know it. Now the knowledge of evil [came] from the transgression of the commandment; into which he would not have fallen, had he been willing not to eat. For by following the Lord without discrimination he was finding the good itself: by passing over the commandment, conscious of himself, he came to know evil. Therefore to follow the commandment simply is good: to pass it over by desiring more is shown to be evil. For by mistrusting the Lord's words he passed over the precept. And now the knowledge of good and evil began to exist, by his reflecting on what he had done. From this entanglement the commandment was freeing him. So, his reasonings showing [it to him], conscious of his evil, he fled; and from the highest wisdom he was reduced to such folly that he thought that by hiding under a tree he could escape the notice of God, the founder of all things, by whom the leaves of all the trees and the tresses of the grasses are numbered; and who said of us that even our hairs are numbered. Into such evil did he run who began to have knowledge of evil and good! From such evil God was freeing [him] at the time when he forbade!

XIV. Now that it has been made plain that he did not forbid eating out of envy, it remains to show that he did not take away deity out of envy: which, however, is easily proved by our demonstrating that it has been restored. For from the beginning of creation up to the condemnation to death, we have recognised that God made all things rightly. Yet the deed of man seems to have shut out God's purpose; since he made [us] that we might be, but it came about, through fault, that we should not be. And if the matter had stood so far that we should not be, the purpose of him who made [us] would have been overcome. But if [man] returns, sin is overcome by the calling back, and the thing is restored to that very end for which it was made; so that the Lord prevails over man's deed, and is not overcome. And his power also requires this, that he be shown to be almighty. For if there is anything he could not do, his diminished power excludes omnipotence: but omnipotence prevails over all things: and since it prevails over all things, it must prevail in this very thing too, that he who made from nothing should call back from death.

XV. It was necessary, therefore, that we return to what we were. But let us inquire how. That first ungrateful one was condemned, who, called to repentance, did not obey. Yet he lived for some time after the sentence, because God foresaw by his foreknowledge that from these very ones righteous men were to be begotten: nor was it just that one should be dissolved at once who held the hope of begetting the righteous: and those who are begotten righteous show that it was not nature that sinned but the will; since, though born of the same parents, they themselves keep the commandments: nor is the will a part of the natural substance, but a movement; yet a movement acting as an indicator of the thoughts, by associating [itself] with something. Now these righteous men of whom we have spoken [are] of the same parents in nature, but unlike them in conduct, through repenting. And justice demands to pass over the unrepentant, and to grant pardon to the penitent. The order of repentance proceeds thus, that it has an effect by which, pleasing God and hoping in his power, it asks for grace. The petition calls upon its creator for absolution; nor does it follow that another grants [it] by calling back, but he who made [us]. For if he made [us] that we might be, but it came about that we should not be, he who restores to eternity would be better than he who made what fell. Therefore to renew belongs to God the creator himself; and he who made from nothing calls back even from the dead. He is invoked to grant [this], and to teach how the grace to be granted may be kept, lest so great a gift be lost: and again so that man, feeling himself freed from the present sentence, as he was before condemned, may differ in his way of life, by using which, in imitating God, he may come to deity; and the deity which he formerly thought he had seized for himself through the tree without God, this he may receive from God himself. For I too have said, You are gods, and all sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes. He who complains that they have lost what he spoke [of] is thereby proved not to have taken away deity out of spite before: and he who complained came, when asked, to grant that very thing which we lost; by showing himself, speaking, granting, calling back.

XVI. Yet it offends some that [he came] in a body: but he would not have been seen by men otherwise than in a body; nor could they have seen their own preservation except in a body. Indeed, he ought not to have freed [us] from the condemnation of death otherwise than in a body, so that he might show freed that very thing which had perished. But let us see how. The woman sinned first, and she sinned while she was a virgin. This cause made all who were born afterwards mortal. For a virgin received the sentence; having been made mortal by it, she procreated the rest as mortals. Through this virgin death held dominion. For this reason he who was to give life had to come through a virgin. The occasion of death entered through wood, but the woman [came] from the side of the man. Therefore the Lord’s side is struck with wood, so that he may suffer for the woman too. And the woman was not the whole side, but a portion of the side: for one of the ribs was taken and built up. Therefore not the whole side is opened, but the very place of the side from which she was taken is pierced. By the sentence of condemnation the earth produced thorns and thistles: therefore he is crowned with thorns and thistles; the substance of thorns, accursed. The crown was a form of victory: and so, by passing through those things through which sin began to be, the Lord triumphed.

XVII. To those who look at human things, what is said seems impossible: that he who was to be born is proclaimed to have been born against nature from a virgin. This does not fall within human reason, that he should be born thus, unlike the rest, and be a son from a mother without a father. Yet this is most fitting for him, that he who has a heavenly father should not have an earthly father. Nor had he come to deny his father by being born of another; but, as to what was lacking in the nature of the begetter, a virgin is his mother. Nor ought the procreator of all to be bound under this condition of our generation, since even the first authors [of our race] were not generated from intercourse. There are also many kinds of begetting things in the world which are generated secretly, in many ways, without union. But the account of the conception, to one who examines it carefully, is possible. He who is holy is proclaimed to have been born of the Holy Spirit: nothing incredible. But his holiness seems to be defiled by mingling; yet there is no mingling. For when the virgin asked and sought the causes of the conception, the angel Gabriel said: The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. In neither does he name mingling; but by the coming of the Spirit, by the power of the Most High, the nature is curdled, so that what in others seed brings about, by the joining of something holier, as befits God, he might be born through the undefiled body of the virgin.

XVIII. Nor is this found to be incredible, since in the world itself we know that very many things are compacted in this way. When the sea was struck with a rod as the Jews crossed, the sea was indeed divided by force; but the wind, the spirit of the world, compacted the waves, as Scripture shows, which says thus: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and the Lord drove the sea with a strong south wind all night, and made the sea dry. It was not, of course, emptied of water, but compacted. For it says: and the water was divided; and the sons of Israel went in through the midst of the sea on dry ground; and the water was a wall to them on the right and on the left. Thus we are taught that what was brought about through the south wind was compacted. And the prophet David the psalmist too, interpreting this very sign, says: He broke open the sea and carried them across; he set the waters like a wineskin. And if anyone, through weakness of mind, preparing hardness of heart for himself, does not believe these proofs, let him examine the force of the winds, and understand that the airs of the world do this very thing: they so compact the rain running down in drippings that it freezes in the very act of falling. Why need we list the other things which, formed from moisture, are solidified by the aforesaid force? Nor is there need to linger long, since the effects of things cry out louder than our assertions. If these things happen in nature at God’s ordaining, how much more, at his so necessary coming, could the body of the virgin, from which [a flow] was expected, be compacted by the Holy Spirit for the forming of the body to be assumed?

XIX. This indeed seems unclean to some, but to those who examine it rightly it is thus proved clean. Before the body’s flux, while it is still constituted part of the body, mingled and compacted with the whole, it does not receive the name of unclean, since it lives. But when it has flowed away and become dead from that [state], then [it is] unclean and dead, because it is now foreign to nature and cannot be brought to life. While it is in nature, compacted and curdled, it generates, and is not unclean. Thus truth finds that it was not unclean. And even if we allow those who call it unclean, it is still clear that holiness could not have been defiled by the unclean. For we see the sun, which we cannot deny is his creature, so act upon the uncleanness of filth, the foul waters of marshes, the rottenness of mud, that though it sends its force upon these through its rays, it is still not polluted. And if the creature is not polluted among these filthy things, much less is divinity itself polluted in a living, holy body.

XX. Now that the holy and undefiled birth through the form of a body, in which the plan of our salvation required [him] to be present, has necessarily been made plain, it remains to prove why, born a little child after our likeness, he grew, hungered, ate, thirsted, and took on the other functions of the body, so that he even suffered death, and so shameful a death; after which death (a thing incredible to those who resist) he is said, having been buried, to have risen again. And indeed it is evident that he who came in the flesh as saviour of the flesh had to take up our [flesh], not another’s: for if another’s were taken up, the salvation would not pertain to us. And having taken up our flesh, he had to be born a little child from a virgin: for it was not fitting that a grown man be born through a virgin, as is shown thus. He would have been said to be born, yet not proved born: for how could a grown man be born through a virgin? So you, who do not believe that he was born a little child, would much less have believed that a man was brought forth.

XXI. Yet let us recognise how divine his littleness is. He was conceived as a man, but without the origin of human seed. He was born as a man, but from a virgin, which is holy. Lowly and unsightly, but glorious: in nature an infant laid in a cradle, but announced by angels as king and Son of God: saviour of the human race, uniter of heaven and earth, maker of glory and peace. This is most plainly taught to the shepherds. For it is written thus: And it came about that while they were there (he means in Bethlehem) her days (that is, Mary’s) were fulfilled for her to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son, and they wrapped him and laid him in a manger, because there was no room in the inn. And there were shepherds in that region spending the night and keeping the night watches over their flocks. And an angel of the Lord stood [by them], and brightness shone around them, and they feared with great fear. And the angel said to them: Do not fear; for see, I announce to you great joy, which is for all the people; for there is born to you today a saviour, who is Christ Jesus, in the city of David. And this [is] the sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in cloths and laid in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good decree. One angel announces the birth: that this one, who was born before the world, is born to us today as a little child, because he then began to exist for men. And lest he seem to be announced as king only of those to whom it was said, is born to you today, the host of angels runs together and says: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good decree. This glory of his appeared in heaven, and peace on earth to men of good decree is announced by angels. Do you notice whether these things seem like our infancy, or not?

XXII. Or is it surprising that angels announced the king whom the Magi too, living in a far-off land, knew? When a sign had appeared to them from heaven, they understood that he was born, found him whom they had long sought, and worshipped him when found. The sign of this star surpassed the other marks of the stars: for the star which was the indicator of the Lord’s birth did not shine like the others in darkness, but gleamed by day in the sun, surpassing both sun and day in splendour; not as one fixed in the sky, but going ahead with marvellous appearance, it showed the way on the journey to those travelling in search of the Lord. Finally it stood over the house, where it showed that he whom it announced was. Scripture attests this: When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, see, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who is born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him. When the Magi saw him, a little child, they worshipped him as king, as man, as God; and they offered gifts, and by these gifts it was also announced that he would suffer. For they offered incense as to God, gold as to a king, myrrh to one who would suffer. Such an infancy is recognised as divine, is nourished, and is brought up! But [he was] knowing all things without a guide. The Jews marvel at this, seeing him know letters without teaching, and saying: How does this man know letters, who has not learned? They confessed that he knew, and did not deny that he had not learned, yet did not grasp whence he had this. When he speaks with the teachers of the Jews, he is found to be teacher of teachers. When, still a little boy of about twelve years, he sat in the midst of the masters, the teachers marvelled at his teaching with amazement. For so Scripture says: And all who heard him marvelled at his understanding and his answers. These things are proved by the scriptures, but more is found by physical reasonings: for God, born in man, had to display such marks of his infancy.

XXIII. But if you ask the reason for his coming, it was necessary that he appear again as a man. So great a divinity had to be hidden, not from those who believed, but from the prince of the world, for whose overthrow he had come down, but for the sake of our liberation. For that [prince] held [men] not by his own authority but by the Lord's sentence, because [the Lord] had ordered that the sinner who did not repent should die. But the merciful one had to set free the one who repents. Justice required this, and divine power required this: that he who held the guilty by the sentence should, if he seized one not guilty, passing beyond the sentence, lose his power. Yet no one is not guilty, since both by origin and by birth they are from mortals. But he who was born is proved to have himself given the sentence; and by that sentence he himself is not held guilty, who, when he had taken up flesh, lived among men without sin. As it is written: This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found every way of understanding, and gave it to Jacob his servant. After these things he was seen on earth, and lived among men. This is he who lived without sin, as again it is written: Who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. This flesh he brought forth without sin; and the prince of this world, foreseeing that it opposed him and was not inclined to his wishes, but reckoning it only a man, dared to attack it, since it allowed [him]. And the Lord allowed it, so that the prince might himself be the cause of his own loss; so that he, who had claimed the guilty for himself by the sentence, by usurping this one who was not guilty, going against the sentence by which he held [them], might lose his power. Thus it was a matter of design that he perform the functions of the body, so that he on his part might show that the flesh he had taken up was the same, the one that had earlier been condemned; while the other, seeing the functions of the flesh, might not perceive the deity, and so, going against the sentence of God, might lose his power; because he dared to seek after one whom he saw to be without crime.

XXIV. For this reason, then, it was done: to show the functions of the flesh, yet not to be subject to those functions. To prove the flesh true, he hungered; not so that, overcome by fasting, he should eat. Accordingly, when to prove [it was] our flesh he had fasted beyond the capacity of nature for the space of forty days and nights, he is found indeed to have hungered, but not also to have eaten; as scripture says: And when forty days and forty nights were completed, afterwards he hungered. Yet he did not eat; but he hungered. This was plainly done for this reason: because during the forty days, in which the devil, fighting continually in the desert against the Lord with his temptations, had been overcome, he was not [hungry]; and so that the devil, perceiving God, might not flee away, and so that the so necessary benefits of his passion might not perish, he hungered. Thinking him then weak, [the devil] attacked him again as a man, telling him that at least for the need of his body he should turn stones into bread; and he neither did it nor ate. Thus he hungered for a reason; yet he was not subject to the reason. And not only in this place, but also when the disciples offered bread to him when hungry, and said: Rabbi, eat, he answered: I have food to eat which you do not know. My food is to do the will of him who sent me, to accomplish his work.

XXV. He thirsted, so that through thirst he might show the nature of the body; not because he needed drink, since he himself is the fount of living water. Accordingly, at the [meeting with the] Samaritan woman, where he is found to have thirsted, when he had asked for water, and she, thinking him a Jew, had not given it, he offered the woman water by which she might quench her thirst for ever, as it is written: Jesus was sitting at the well; and it was about the sixth hour; and a certain Samaritan woman came to draw water. And Jesus was sitting; and Jesus said to her: Give me to drink. For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food. But the woman answered Jesus, saying: How do you, being a Jew, ask a drink of me, since I am a Samaritan woman? And Jesus answered her: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who said to you, Give me to drink, you would rather have asked him, and he would have given you living water. And the woman said to him: Lord, you have no pitcher, and the well is deep; from where do you have living water to give me? Surely you are not greater than our father Jacob, since he gave us the well from which he drank with his sons and with his cattle. And Jesus answered her: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him will not thirst for ever; but it will be a fount of water springing up into eternal life. So he had not thirsted to receive but to give, he who gave the divine [water] by promising it, so that the woman, leaving her water jar, forgetting her old thirst, proclaimed his coming to the other Samaritans of Samaria. This is what the Lord thirsted for: to teach the woman, whom he already knew to be ready; not seeking earthly water, but by his request giving living water, which made a fount springing up into eternal life.

XXVI. Again Jesus thirsted on the cross, and cried out: I thirst. But the cause of his thirst was this. They had crucified him, and yet were not thus sated: they still had sin to commit. And although compassion, the feeling of common nature, is owed even to wicked men placed under punishment, they, against the natural motion of compassion, insulted even after the cross this one whose benefits they had felt in the healing of infirmities, and whom they had assailed without crime; so filled were they with the spirit of fury that they gave him vinegar to drink when he thirsted. And he who had undertaken the passion with a ready mind did not accept this unwillingly either; and as much as they were bolder in inflicting tortures, so much was he gentle in undergoing injury. Seeing that the works of their malice were not yet complete, he cried out: I thirst. And they, to heap up the injury, gave vinegar; yet he did not provoke them to force vinegar on him, but what they gave him he accepted of his own accord. Such was the Lord's thirst. Then, having received it, he cried out: It is finished. And at once he gave up his spirit. Jesus also slept, not overcome by sleep, as it might seem, but so that there might be an order for a mighty work to be done. For he slept so that the sea might be stirred up, so that the disciples in fear might ask for help, so that the prophecy of David might be fulfilled, which he pronounced in the hundred and sixth psalm, saying: Let his works be proclaimed with rejoicing. Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business on many waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and the wind of the storm stood up, and its waves were lifted high. And that he would complete the whole dispensation, by so acting, through death, and would ascend to the heavens, [the psalm] at once added, saying: He goes up to the heavens, and goes down to the depths.

XXVII. And although this, said by the divine Spirit, is to be believed, yet, like the other things, let us also prove this by a few physical reasonings. Having freed us from death by the Lord's passion, he led us again to the state of immortality; and us, formerly unequal to the heavenly [beings], he has now joined to the heavenly. To some, however, this seems unjust; not because God cannot [do it], but because it seems not to befit his justice that, whereas he had made the first-formed, while still free of fault and a stranger to crime, lord only of paradise, judging this gift of God fitting, now, after he was recalled after sin and offence, although it was no small thing to have returned to what he had been, he should also have granted the heavenly kingdoms. Yet this is proved most just. For if before, by his grace, he had granted man the seat of paradise when he had deserved it by no duties of devotion, surely now, when [man] had already been set in motion against the impatience of the flesh and the desires of iniquity, fighting against the prince of the world and his powers, having trampled on the world, it was fitting to repay a heavenly reward; so that he who, by imitating God, led a divine life on earth while placed in the body, might dwell in the heavens with that same body now made immortal, earthly things now taken away. Next, to the reason for this gift is added this: that it is fitting to bring into the heavens the flesh of man, of which God deigned to be the inhabitant; nor can it seem that man has been made a dweller in heaven against his merit, whose sheath the Spirit, God himself, did not disdain. And it was just that the body in which God, by dwelling, deigned to visit the earth, through which, as a sharer in our [nature], he led our race to immortality, should also be placed among the heavenly. For where should God's dwelling be, if not in the kingdom of God? And where is his kingdom, if not in the heavens?
